explain.text:
Figure 1 shows two plots from the same experiment: CIFAR-10 trained with "plain" networks (no shortcuts) of 20 and 56 layers. The x-axis is training iterations in units of 10,000, running to about 6 (roughly 60k). The left panel plots training error, the right panel plots test error, both in percent.

In both panels the red 56-layer curve sits above the yellow-green 20-layer curve for the whole run. By the end, the 56-layer net has a training error of roughly 6%, against about 1.5% for the 20-layer net. Test error ends near 13% for the 56-layer net and about 10% for the 20-layer net. Both curves drop sharply near 3.2 iterations (x1e4), which matches the learning-rate cut described for CIFAR-10 at 32k iterations p. 7.

The point is in the left panel. A deeper network is a bigger model, so you would expect it to fit the training data at least as well. Instead it fits worse. The document calls this the degradation problem and says it is not caused by overfitting, because overfitting would show low training error with high test error p. 1. The higher test error on the right is therefore a consequence of the higher training error, as the caption says.

ask.text:
In the right panel, the 56-layer curve (red) ends at about 13%, while the 20-layer curve (yellow-green) ends at about 9.5 to 10%. So the deeper network is worse by roughly 3 to 3.5 percentage points.

The gap is there for most of the run. Both curves fall sharply near 3.2 on the x-axis (3.2e4 iterations), and afterward they flatten out roughly parallel, with the 56-layer net staying above the 20-layer one the whole way.

The figure only gives these values by eye from the curves. The document does not print exact numbers for these two plain networks in the text, though the caption says the deeper network has higher training error and thus higher test error p. 1. The later CIFAR-10 experiments on page 7 cover the same depth comparison with plain nets in Fig. 6 p. 7.

explain.text:
The image shows the output end of the building block in Fig. 2: the expression F(x) + x, then a circled plus (the addition node) with an arrow entering from the right, followed by relu below it.

F(x) is the output of the stacked weight layers, which the paper defines as the residual F(x) := H(x) − x, where H(x) is the mapping those layers would otherwise be asked to fit. The arrow from the right is the shortcut carrying x unchanged, an identity mapping. The two are added element-wise, so the block outputs F(x) + x, which recovers the desired H(x). The relu applied after the addition is the second nonlinearity p. 3.

The motivation is that if an identity mapping were optimal, it would be easier to push the residual toward zero than to fit an identity with a stack of nonlinear layers p. 2. The shortcut adds no parameters or computation p. 2.

The paper's formal version is eq. 1 on page 3, y = F(x, {Wi}) + x. It does not explain the arrow directions in the figure beyond this.

ask.text:
Right after the addition, the summed signal passes through a ReLU, shown by the arrow pointing down from the circled plus to "relu". The paper describes this as adopting the second nonlinearity after the addition, so the block's output is σ(y), where y = F(x) + x p. 3. Here σ is ReLU, which sets negative values to zero and leaves positive values unchanged.

In the image, you can also see two arrows feeding the plus node: one entering from the top (the output of the stacked weight layers, F(x)) and one from the right (the identity shortcut carrying x). The label "F(x) + x" beside the node names the sum that is being formed.

Worth noting: the ReLU sits outside the shortcut path. The shortcut itself is a plain identity, with no nonlinearity applied to x before it is added. The nonlinearity only acts once the two are combined. The paper does not say why it chose this placement over others, beyond stating that this is what it adopts.

explain.text:
Figure 3 puts three architectures side by side, all taking an image in and ending in a 1000-way classifier.

Left is VGG-19, the reference at 19.6 billion FLOPs. It uses stacks of 3x3 convolutions with 64, 128, 256, 512 and 512 filters, and max pooling (pool, /2) between stages to halve the feature map from 224 down to 7. It ends with two fc 4096 layers and fc 1000.

Middle is the 34-layer plain network. It starts with a 7x7 conv, 64, /2, then a pool, then 3x3 convs in four stages of 64, 128, 256 and 512 filters. Downsampling is done by convs with stride 2 (the "/2" boxes), not pooling. It finishes with global average pooling and a single fc 1000. That gives 3.6 billion FLOPs, about 18% of VGG-19 p. 3.

Right is the same network with shortcut arrows added around each pair of 3x3 layers. Solid arrows are identity shortcuts. Dotted arrows appear where the number of filters increases (64 to 128, 128 to 256, 256 to 512), so dimensions must be matched, either by zero-padding (option A) or 1x1 projection (option B) p. 4.

The dotted shortcuts add no FLOPs under option A, which is why both networks are listed at 3.6 billion.

ask.text:
The dotted arrows mark shortcuts where the dimensions increase. In the figure, each one jumps over a block whose first conv has a stride of 2 and doubles the filter count (the "3x3 conv, 128, /2", "256, /2" and "512, /2" boxes). There the input x and the output of the stacked layers no longer have matching shapes, so the plain identity addition of eq. 1 cannot be used. The document offers two fixes: option A keeps the identity and pads extra zero entries, and option B uses the projection W_s of eq. 2, done with 1x1 convolutions. In both, the shortcut goes across feature maps of two sizes with a stride of 2 p. 4. Solid arrows are plain identity shortcuts.

Counting the dotted arrows in the right-hand column, there are three: one into the 128-filter stage, one into the 256-filter stage, and one into the 512-filter stage. The first stage (64 filters) needs none because the pooling layer before it already gives matching dimensions.

This count matches the text's remark that option C, which makes all shortcuts projections, involves thirteen projection shortcuts p. 6. Those thirteen would be the three dotted ones plus the ten solid ones in the right column, giving sixteen in total, so the figure and text are consistent with 16 shortcuts overall.

explain.text:
Figure 4 shows ImageNet training curves, with iterations (in units of 1e4) on the x-axis and error (%) on the y-axis, which runs from 20 to 60. Thin curves are training error and bold curves are validation error on center crops. Cyan is the 18-layer net and red is the 34-layer net.

On the left, the plain nets show the degradation problem. The 34-layer plain net sits above the 18-layer one for essentially the whole run, in both training and validation error. The document points out this happens even though the 18-layer net's solution space is a subspace of the 34-layer one p. 5.

On the right, the order flips for the ResNets. The 34-layer ResNet ends up below the 18-layer one, with clearly lower training error, so the extra depth now helps. The document reports the 34-layer ResNet beating the 18-layer by 2.8% and the 34-layer plain net by 3.5% p. 6.

The sharp drops at roughly 15 and 30 on the x-axis are consistent with the learning rate being divided by 10 when error plateaus p. 4, though the figure itself doesn't label them.

The right panel also shows the 18-layer ResNet dropping faster early on, which matches the faster convergence the document notes p. 6.

ask.text:
In both panels the sharp drops fall at about 15 and 30 on the x-axis. Since the axis is in units of 1e4, that is roughly 150,000 and 300,000 iterations. You can see the curves fall almost vertically at those two points, then flatten into a plateau until the next one.

The figure doesn't label the cause, and the caption doesn't mention it. The likely explanation comes from the training recipe in the text: the learning rate starts at 0.1 and is divided by 10 when the error plateaus p. 4. A step-down in learning rate typically produces exactly this pattern, a sudden drop followed by a flat stretch. The document doesn't say the drops line up with those schedule changes or give the exact iterations at which it reduced the rate, so treat that link as my inference. The plateaus before each drop fit the "when the error plateaus" trigger, though.

The text does say training runs for up to 60 × 10^4 iterations p. 4, and the plotted curves end near 55.

explain.text:
Table 8 is the small two-row table at the lower right of the image. It compares two backbones inside the same Faster R-CNN detector on the COCO validation set. VGG-16 scores 41.5 on mAP@.5 and 21.2 on mAP@[.5, .95]. ResNet-101 scores 48.4 and 27.2, shown in bold.

The two metrics differ in how strict they are. mAP@.5 counts a detection as correct if its box overlaps the true box by at least 0.5 IoU. mAP@[.5, .95] averages over IoU thresholds from .5 to .95 in steps of .05, so it rewards tighter localization. The appendix states this on p. 10.

The text on p. 8 reads the table this way: the detection implementation is identical for both networks, so the gain comes only from the better network. The 6.0 point rise in mAP@[.5, .95] is the 28% relative improvement (6.0 / 21.2). The appendix adds that this absolute gain is nearly as large as the 6.9 point gain at mAP@.5, which it takes to suggest that a deeper network improves both recognition and localization p. 10.

The other panels in the image are Figure 6 (CIFAR-10 training curves), Figure 7 (layer response standard deviations), and Table 7 (PASCAL VOC results), which are separate from Table 8.

ask.text:
In the right panel of Figure 6, the 1202-layer network (residual-1202) is drawn in magenta, while residual-110 is black. The bold magenta line, which is test error, sits a little under 8% for most of the run, roughly 7.5 to 8.5% and ending near 8%. That matches the 7.93% the paper reports for ResNet-1202 p. 7. The black 110-layer curve is lower, at about 6.5%, consistent with its reported 6.43% p. 7.

The dashed magenta line near the bottom is the 1202-layer training error, which is close to zero. The text says it reaches below 0.1% p. 8. The paper attributes the gap between the two to overfitting, since 19.4M parameters is probably more than this small dataset needs p. 8.

ask.text:
In the bottom plot of Figure 7, where layer responses are sorted by magnitude, ResNet-110 (the black curve) has the smallest responses overall. Its std drops to roughly 1 by about layer 20 and then slides down gradually to a bit under 1, around 0.7 at the far end, across about 110 layers. The other curves sit above it over the range they cover: the dashed plain-56 line starts near 2.5 and stays well above 1 for much of its length, and plain-20 and ResNet-20 are higher than ResNet-110 at comparable indices.

ResNet-56 (red) is close to ResNet-110 and also ends below 1, but it stays slightly higher over most of its range.

This matches what the paper says: ResNets have generally smaller responses than their plain counterparts, and deeper ResNets have smaller magnitudes, as seen comparing ResNet-20, 56, and 110 p. 8. The authors read this as each layer in a deeper ResNet tending to modify the signal less p. 8.
